concepts.title: Historical Time: BCE and CE
concepts.section: How do we measure historical time
concepts.definition: History measures time on a shared timeline: years are counted backwards from the birth of Christ as BCE and forwards as CE, so events can be placed in order across centuries and millennia.
concepts.key_idea: A common timeline lets people everywhere agree on when things happened, long before clocks or calendars.

concepts.title: Sources of History
concepts.definition: Historians read the past through sources: material remains such as pottery, coins and monuments, written records such as manuscripts and inscriptions, and oral traditions passed by word of mouth.
concepts.key_idea: Each source is a thread; woven together they form the tapestry of the past.

concepts.title: Museums: Homes of the Past
concepts.definition: Museums such as the National Museum in New Delhi collect and preserve objects from the past, statues, coins and ornaments, keeping them safe so that everyone can study and enjoy them.
concepts.key_idea: A museum is a library of things: each object on display is a source you can see and touch with your eyes.

concepts.title: The Present and the Past
concepts.definition: E. H. Carr calls history an unending dialogue between the present and the past; we understand today's society only in the light of yesterday's, and each generation asks the past fresh questions.
concepts.key_idea: Studying the past is a conversation: present questions bring old answers to life again.

worked_examples.question_pattern: Why is a coin a good source of history?

solution_template.explain: A coin carries the mark of its ruler, its metal and its date.
From one small disc we learn who ruled, what they valued and how trade moved.

worked_examples.question_pattern: How do BCE years count backwards?

solution_template.explain: On the timeline, years before Christ are counted backwards towards larger BCE numbers.
So 500 BCE is earlier than 200 BCE, while CE years grow forward like ordinary counting.
